props.title: Color Me Blood Red

sections.content: **Color Me Blood Red** (1965) stands as Herschell Gordon Lewis's grotesque finale to his "Blood Trilogy," following Blood Feast (1963) and Two Thousand Maniacs! (1964). This lurid tale of a frustrated artist who discovers human blood makes the perfect red paint pushes exploitation cinema into art-world satire territory. Lewis, nicknamed the "Godfather of Gore," crafted this twisted commentary on artistic obsession while pioneering practical effects techniques that would influence directors like Tom Savini and Rob Zombie decades later.

sections.content: Lewis's influence rippled through horror cinema, inspiring a wave of art-themed horror films. **The Driller Killer** (1979) similarly follows a disturbed painter driven to murder, while **Bucket of Blood** (1959) presents a twisted take on sculpture. More recently, **Velvet Buzzsaw** (2019) and **Nocturnal Animals** (2016) continue exploring the intersection of art and violence, though with considerably larger budgets than Lewis's $50,000 exploitation classic. SUBHEAD: The Art of Gore and Social Commentary

While dismissed by critics at release, **Color Me Blood Red** (1965) cleverly skewers the pretensions of the art world while delivering the shocking gore Lewis's audiences demanded. The film's premise - an artist literally bleeding his subjects dry for his art - works as both exploitation shock and metaphor for artistic vampirism. Later films like **The House That Jack Built** (2018) and **Neon Demon** (2016) would explore similar themes of art, death, and obsession with more philosophical weight but arguably less raw impact.
